subtitle: Build fake data, run Monte Carlo experiments, check your intuition.

code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(2024)
print(rng.integers(1, 7, size=5))   # [2 5 1 2 2]

rng = np.random.default_rng(2024)   # same seed
print(rng.integers(1, 7, size=5))   # [2 5 1 2 2]  -- identical
caption: integers(1, 7) excludes the upper bound -- a six-sided die. Same seed, same "random" numbers.

code:
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "visits": rng.poisson(3, n),
    "order_value": rng.lognormal(3.5, 0.6, n).round(2),
    "returned": rng.binomial(1, 0.3, n),
    "delivery_min": rng.normal(40, 5, n).round(1),
})
# means land near 3, 39, 0.30, 40 -- max order value: 668 (log-normal tail)
caption: Great for practicing pandas or testing a pipeline before real data arrives.

code:
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(100_000, 2)).sum(axis=1)
print(round((rolls >= 10).mean(), 4))   # 0.1653 -- exact answer: 0.1667
caption: Repeat a random experiment many times and count -- for when no simple formula exists.

eyebrow: A real question: how risky is daily kept revenue?
code:
vals = rng.lognormal(3.5, 0.6, size=(days, 50))   # 50 orders/day
returned = rng.random((days, 50)) < 0.3
kept = np.where(returned, 0, vals).sum(axis=1)
# mean 1389.0, 5th pct 1073.3, P(kept < 1000) = 0.0176
caption: Each row = one simulated day, vectorized -- far faster than a Python loop.

eyebrow: More draws, more accuracy -- but slowly
caption: Error shrinks with the square root of draws -- quadrupling draws only halves the noise.
